title: Banana Spelt Choc Chip Muffins
seoTitle: Banana Spelt Choc Chip Muffins (Dairy Free)
metaDesc: These easy banana spelt choc chip muffins are dairy free, nut free, and naturally sweetened. Made with organic spelt flour and ripe bananas. Ready in 35 minutes.
about: These nourishing banana muffins are a staple in our kitchen. Made with organic spelt flour, naturally sweetened with ripe bananas and a touch of maple syrup, and loaded with dairy free choc chips, they are completely dairy free and nut free. We make a batch on Sunday and they are gone by Tuesday. These banana spelt choc chip muffins are a Sunday staple in our house. We make a batch every week and they are gone by Tuesday, which tells you everything you need to know. Made with organic spelt flour, naturally sweetened with ripe bananas and a touch of maple syrup, and packed with dairy free choc chips, they are completely dairy free and nut free, so they are perfect for lunchboxes too.
chefNote: Spelt flour absorbs liquid a little differently to plain wheat flour, so make sure you do not overmix the batter or your muffins can turn dense. These muffins freeze beautifully. Once completely cooled, pop them into a zip lock bag or airtight container and freeze for up to 3 months. Pull one out the night before and it will be ready by morning.
servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature as an after school snack or lunchbox treat. They are also lovely lightly warmed with a drizzle of extra maple syrup for a special weekend breakfast.

ingredients.name: melted coconut oil, plus extra for greasing
unsweetened oat milk or coconut milk
dairy free dark choc chips, plus extra for topping

steps: Preheat your oven to 180 degrees Celsius fan forced. Grease a 12 hole muffin tin generously with coconut oil or line with paper cases.
Peel and mash the ripe bananas in a large mixing bowl until smooth. The riper the bananas, the sweeter and more flavourful your muffins will be.
Add the eggs, maple syrup, melted coconut oil, oat milk, and vanilla extract to the mashed banana. Whisk everything together until well combined.
In a separate bowl, sift together the spelt flour, baking powder, bicarbonate of soda, cinnamon, and sea salt. Give it a quick stir to make sure everything is evenly distributed.
Pour the wet ingredients into the dry ingredients and fold gently with a spatula until just combined. Do not overmix. A few small lumps are perfectly fine and will keep your muffins light and tender.
Fold through three quarters of the choc chips, reserving the rest for the tops.
Divide the batter evenly between the 12 muffin holes, filling each one about three quarters full. Scatter the remaining choc chips over the top of each muffin.
Bake for 18 to 22 minutes, or until a skewer inserted into the centre of a muffin comes out clean and the tops are lightly golden.
Remove the tin from the oven and allow the muffins to cool in the tin for 5 minutes before transferring to a wire rack to cool completely. They firm up as they cool, so be patient before diving in.
author: Mr Wellness

title: Chickpea & Green Bean Curry
seoTitle: Chickpea & Green Bean Curry, Pristine Wellness
about: A deeply nourishing, plant-based curry that celebrates the anti-inflammatory power of turmeric and the wholesome goodness of chickpeas, a staple in our family kitchen.
chefNote: Toast your dry spices in the pan for 30 seconds before adding the onion. The heat releases the essential oils and transforms the dish entirely.

steps.title: Toast the spices
steps.text: Heat a large pan over medium heat. Add turmeric, cumin, garam masala and coriander directly to the dry pan. Toast for 30 seconds, stirring constantly, until fragrant.

steps.title: Sauté the aromatics
steps.text: Add olive oil or coconut oil. Add diced onion and cook for 5,6 minutes until soft. Add minced garlic and cook for a further 2 minutes.

steps.title: Build the sauce
steps.text: Add crushed tomatoes and stir well. Cook for 3,4 minutes until tomatoes deepen in colour and the oil begins to separate around the edges.

steps.title: Add chickpeas & coconut milk
steps.text: Add drained chickpeas and coconut milk. Stir to combine and bring to a gentle simmer. Cook uncovered for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally.

steps.title: Add green beans & finish
steps.text: Add trimmed green beans and cook for a final 5 minutes until just tender but still vibrant green. Taste and season. Serve over basmati rice with lime and fresh coriander.

author: Mr Wellness

title: Creamy Cauliflower Soup
metaDesc: A simple, nourishing creamy cauliflower soup made with real chicken stock and pure cream. Gluten free, egg free and nut free. Ready in under 40 minutes.
about: This is the kind of soup we return to again and again through the cooler months, simple enough for a weeknight but nourishing enough to feel like real care on a plate. Cauliflower is rich in sulforaphane and vitamin C, and when it is simmered gently with good chicken stock and finished with cream, it becomes something quietly luxurious. We love that it comes together with just a handful of honest ingredients and rewards you with a bowlful that genuinely satisfies.
chefNote: Homemade chicken bone broth makes a meaningful difference to the depth of flavour here, and it adds a generous dose of natural gelatin and minerals that a commercial stock simply cannot match. If you are using store-bought stock, choose a low-sodium variety so you can control the seasoning yourself. Leftover soup keeps well in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days, or can be frozen in portions for up to three months. Reheat gently over low heat, stirring often, and add a small splash of water or stock if it has thickened during storage.
servingSuggestion: Serve in deep bowls with a drizzle of good olive oil and a crack of black pepper over the top. A thick slice of sourdough or seeded rye bread alongside makes this a complete and satisfying meal, and a small handful of finely sliced chives scattered over the soup adds a gentle fresh note that works beautifully with the cream.

ingredients.name: potatoes, peeled and chopped into rough chunks
good quality chicken stock, preferably homemade (see Chef Note)

steps: Place a large, heavy-based saucepan over medium-high heat and add the olive oil, allowing it to warm for about thirty seconds before adding the chopped onion and crushed garlic. Cook, stirring regularly, for around three minutes until the onion has softened and turned translucent and the garlic smells fragrant. Add the cauliflower florets and chopped potato to the pan and continue stirring everything together for five minutes, allowing the vegetables to begin softening and to absorb the flavour from the onion and garlic in the base of the pot.

Pour in the chicken stock, then season generously with freshly ground black pepper. Place the lid on the saucepan and bring everything up to the boil over medium-high heat, then reduce the heat to medium-low and leave the soup to simmer steadily for fifteen to twenty minutes, or until a piece of potato yields easily when pressed with a spoon. Remove the pan from the heat and set it aside for five minutes so the soup cools slightly before blending, which makes the process safer and easier.

Working in batches if needed, carefully ladle the soup into a blender and blend each batch until completely smooth, then return the blended soup to the saucepan. If you have a stick blender you can blend directly in the pot, which saves on washing up. Place the pan back over low heat, pour in the pure cream and stir gently for about two minutes until the soup is heated through and the cream is fully incorporated. Taste and adjust seasoning if needed, then ladle into warm bowls and serve straight away.

title: Fermented Overnight Oats with Raw Honey and Seasonal Fruit
seoTitle: Fermented Overnight Oats with Raw Honey
metaDesc: Oats soaked overnight in an acidic medium to break down phytic acid, making vitamins and minerals far easier to absorb. Topped with raw honey and seasonal fruit.
about: Soaked, fermented, wholefood school-morning fuel no refined sugar needed
chefNote: If your family is new to fermented grains, start with just one tablespoon of apple cider vinegar and build up over a few days. You can prep four individual jars on Sunday night and refrigerate after the overnight soak and rinse, then add toppings fresh each morning. Oats keep well in the fridge for up to three days once drained.
servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a glass of raw whole milk or a simple green smoothie for a complete wholefood school morning breakfast. A soft boiled egg on the side adds extra protein for bigger appetites.

ingredients.name: raw apple cider vinegar (with the mother) or plain full-fat yoghurt
full-fat organic milk or coconut milk
raw honey, plus extra to drizzle
full-fat Greek yoghurt or coconut yoghurt, to serve
seasonal fresh fruit, sliced or chopped (strawberries, mango, banana, stone fruit or berries all work beautifully)
activated nuts or seeds of choice (pepitas, sunflower seeds or crushed walnuts)

steps: The evening before, add the rolled oats and filtered water to a large bowl or glass jar. Stir in the raw apple cider vinegar or plain yoghurt. This acidic starter is what begins the fermentation process and unlocks the nutrition locked inside the oats. Cover loosely with a clean cloth or beeswax wrap and leave on the bench at room temperature for at least 8 hours and up to 12 hours overnight.

In the morning, drain the oats through a fine mesh sieve and give them a quick rinse under cool filtered water. This removes the phytates and any bitter taste from the soaking liquid. Do not skip this step.

Transfer the drained oats back into your bowl or a medium saucepan. Pour in the full-fat milk or coconut milk and stir well to combine. The oats will have softened considerably overnight and will absorb the milk beautifully.

Add the raw honey, vanilla extract, ground cinnamon and sea salt. Stir everything together until the honey is dissolved and the oats are evenly coated. If you prefer a warm breakfast, gently heat the oats over low heat for 3 to 5 minutes, stirring frequently, until warmed through. If your household prefers them cold, they are ready to serve as is.

Prepare your seasonal fruit while the oats are warming if needed. Slice strawberries, chop mango, halve grapes or scatter whole blueberries, whatever is in season and what your family loves right now.
Spoon the oats evenly into four bowls. Top each bowl with a generous tablespoon of Greek yoghurt or coconut yoghurt.
Scatter the seasonal fruit over each bowl, then add a tablespoon of activated nuts or seeds for crunch and healthy fats. Sprinkle over a little desiccated coconut.
Finish each bowl with an extra drizzle of raw honey if you like things a touch sweeter. Serve immediately and watch the bowls disappear before you have even sat down yourself.

title: Lamb Liver Pâté with Sourdough Toast
seoTitle: Lamb Liver Pâté with Sourdough Toast
metaDesc: A simple, nutrient-dense lamb liver pâté made with cultured butter and fresh thyme. Ready in under an hour and perfect spread on toasted sourdough.
about: Pasture-raised lamb liver is one of the most nutrient-dense foods we can put on the table, rich in fat-soluble vitamins, iron, and folate in forms the body actually absorbs. We make this pâté often because it comes together quickly, keeps beautifully in the fridge, and the combination of cultured butter and fresh thyme turns something deeply nourishing into something the whole family genuinely looks forward to. Spread thickly on a slice of good sourdough, it is the kind of snack that actually sustains everyone until dinner.
chefNote: The pâté will keep in the fridge for up to four days as long as the butter seal remains intact. If you want a slightly richer flavour, a small splash of brandy or dry sherry added to the pan just before you take it off the heat works beautifully, though the recipe is equally delicious without it.
servingSuggestion: Serve on thick slices of toasted sourdough with a few cornichons or pickled vegetables on the side to cut through the richness. A simple green salad with a sharp vinaigrette rounds it out into a very satisfying light meal.

ingredients.name: pasture-raised lamb liver, trimmed and sinew removed
cultured butter, plus extra for sealing
beef tallow or extra cultured butter, for frying
sea salt, plus more to taste

steps: Begin by soaking the trimmed lamb liver in cold water for 30 minutes, then drain and pat thoroughly dry with paper towel. This short soak draws out any bitterness and gives the finished pâté a cleaner, milder flavour that even hesitant eaters tend to enjoy.

Warm the tallow or a tablespoon of cultured butter in a wide frying pan over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook gently for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it is soft and translucent without taking on much colour. Add the garlic and thyme leaves and cook for another 2 minutes until fragrant.

Increase the heat to medium-high and add the liver pieces in a single layer. Cook for about 2 to 3 minutes per side. You are looking for a light golden colour on the outside while keeping the centre just faintly pink, which keeps the texture smooth and the flavour gentle rather than heavy.

Remove the pan from the heat and allow everything to cool for about 10 minutes. Transferring hot liver directly to a food processor can make the texture grainy, so this short rest makes a real difference to the final result.

Place the cooled liver, onion mixture, and all the pan juices into a food processor. Add the cultured butter, cream or milk, sea salt, and white pepper. Blend on high for about 2 minutes, scraping down the sides once or twice, until the pâté is very smooth and creamy.
Taste the mixture and adjust the seasoning as needed. Spoon the pâté into one larger dish or divide between small ramekins, smoothing the surface with the back of a spoon.

Melt a small knob of extra cultured butter and pour a thin layer over the surface of the pâté to seal it. This not only keeps the pâté looking beautiful but also protects it from oxidising in the fridge. Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes before serving so it firms to a spreadable consistency.
When ready to serve, toast the sourdough slices until golden and crisp. Bring the pâté to the table straight from the fridge and let everyone spread as generously as they like.

title: No Sugar Banana Choc Chip Muffins
seoTitle: No Sugar Banana Choc Chip Muffins
metaDesc: Nourishing spelt flour muffins naturally sweetened with ripe banana and maple syrup. Dairy free, egg free and nut free. A wholefood snack the whole family loves.
about: These nourishing banana muffins are a staple in our kitchen. Made with organic spelt flour, naturally sweetened with ripe bananas and a touch of maple syrup, and loaded with dairy free choc chips, they are completely dairy free and nut free. We make a batch on Sunday and they are gone by Tuesday.
chefNote: Store cooled muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days, or freeze them individually for up to 2 months. Pop one in a lunchbox frozen in the morning and it will be perfectly thawed by recess.

ingredients.name: dairy free organic choc chips, plus extra for topping

steps: Preheat your oven to 180 degrees Celsius fan forced. Line a 12 hole muffin tin with paper cases or grease well with a little olive oil.
In a large mixing bowl, combine the spelt flour, baking soda, ground cinnamon, and sea salt. Stir well to distribute everything evenly.
In a separate bowl, mash your ripe bananas thoroughly with a fork until smooth. The riper the bananas the better, lots of dark spots means lots of natural sweetness.
Add the olive oil, eggs, and maple syrup to the mashed banana. Whisk together until everything is well combined.

Pour the wet banana mixture into the bowl of dry ingredients. Use a wooden spoon or spatula to gently fold everything together. Stop mixing as soon as no dry flour remains. Do not overmix or the muffins will turn out dense.
Fold through the 1 cup of dairy free choc chips gently so they are evenly distributed through the batter.
Spoon the batter evenly into the 12 prepared muffin cases, filling each one about three quarters of the way full.
Scatter a few extra choc chips over the top of each muffin for a beautiful finish.
Bake for 18 to 20 minutes, or until the muffins are golden on top and a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean.
Allow the muffins to cool in the tin for 5 minutes before transferring to a wire rack. They are wonderful warm but also keep really well once fully cooled.
author: Mr Wellness

title: No Wheat Chocolate Mud Cake
seoTitle: No Wheat Chocolate Mud Cake (Gluten Free)
metaDesc: A rich, fudgy gluten free chocolate mud cake made with almond flour. Dairy free, high protein, and naturally sweetened. Our family birthday favourite.
about: This recipe is the cake we eat whe n someonein our house has a birthday its amazing, and can be no sugar depending on what sweetner you decide to use. high in protein and my kids cant get rnough and i dont feel guilty feeding it to them
chefNote: If you prefer maple syrup or honey as your sweetener instead of monk fruit, start with ½ cup and add more to taste before baking, keeping in mind that liquid sweeteners will make the batter slightly looser. The cake keeps well covered in the fridge for up to four days and the texture actually improves overnight as the flavours settle and the crumb firms up just enough to slice beautifully.
servingSuggestion: Serve at room temperature with a scoop of coconut milk ice cream or a dollop of whipped coconut cream on the side. A small handful of fresh berries alongside cuts through the richness of the ganache and makes it feel properly festive for a birthday table.

ingredients.name: monk fruit sweetener (or erythritol blend, or substitute with pure maple syrup or raw honey to taste)
melted coconut oil (or light olive oil)
milk of choice (coconut milk or almond milk both work beautifully)
espresso powder (optional, deepens the chocolate flavour)
dairy free dark chocolate chips (optional, folded through batter)
dairy free dark chocolate (70% or higher), roughly chopped, for ganache
full fat coconut cream, for ganache

steps: Preheat your oven to 175°C (350°F) and position the rack in the centre. Grease an 8 or 9 inch round cake tin with a little coconut oil, then line the base and sides with baking paper so the cake lifts out cleanly once it has cooled.

In a large mixing bowl, combine the almond flour, cocoa powder, monk fruit sweetener, baking soda, salt, and espresso powder if you are using it. Whisk everything together well so there are no lumps of cocoa hiding in the mix, as almond flour can clump and uneven dry ingredients will affect the final texture.

In a separate bowl, whisk together the eggs, melted coconut oil, milk, and vanilla extract until the mixture is smooth and the eggs are fully incorporated. This only takes about a minute by hand and it is worth doing properly so the fat emulsifies evenly through the batter.

Pour the wet ingredients into the bowl of dry ingredients and stir gently with a spatula or wooden spoon until just combined. The batter will be noticeably thicker than a conventional cake batter, and that is exactly right for almond flour. Avoid over-mixing once the flour is incorporated. If you are adding chocolate chips, fold them through now.

Spoon the batter into your prepared tin and use the back of the spatula to smooth the top into an even layer. Because the batter is thick it will not self-level the way a wheat-flour batter does, so a little extra care here gives you a more even crumb once baked.

Bake for 28 to 35 minutes, checking from the 28 minute mark. The cake is ready when the centre looks set rather than glossy and wet, and a toothpick inserted into the middle comes out with just a few moist crumbs clinging to it. Almond flour cakes dry out quickly if overbaked, so pull it from the oven as soon as that test is met rather than waiting for a completely clean skewer.

Allow the cake to cool in the tin for 15 minutes before carefully running a knife around the edge and turning it out onto a wire rack. Let it cool completely before you add any frosting, as a warm almond flour cake is quite delicate and will hold together much better once it has rested fully.

To make the coconut ganache, place the chopped dark chocolate in a heatproof bowl. Warm the coconut cream in a small saucepan over medium heat until it just begins to simmer, then pour it over the chocolate. Let it sit for two minutes without stirring, then gently stir from the centre outward until you have a glossy, smooth ganache. Allow it to cool at room temperature for 20 to 30 minutes until it thickens to a spreadable consistency.

Once the cake is completely cool and the ganache has thickened, spoon the ganache over the top of the cake and use a spatula to spread it to the edges, letting it drip naturally down the sides for a relaxed, celebratory finish. Slice and serve, and try not to be surprised when the birthday person asks for seconds.
author: Mr Wellness

title: Organic Micro Garden Salad
metaDesc: A finely chopped wholefood salad the whole family loves. Every ingredient cut small so each mouthful delivers the perfect balance of flavour, crunch and freshness.
about:
This salad is absolutely delectable. Every time we serve it, someone asks for the recipe. The secret isn't just the ingredients, it's the preparation. Taking the time to finely chop everything creates a salad that's balanced, flavourful and easy to eat.

The idea is simple: treat the salad like a rice dish. Every ingredient is cut small so each mouthful delivers the perfect mix of textures and flavours. It works beautifully as a side dish, but it's equally satisfying on its own.

Even kids who normally avoid salad seem to enjoy this one. Once you try it, you'll understand why it's become a favourite at our table.
chefNote: A sharp knife is the single most important tool for this recipe. Blunt knives crush and bruise the vegetables rather than cutting them cleanly, which affects both texture and flavour. If you do not have MEA water, filtered water works well. Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to one day, though the texture is always best on the day it is made.
servingSuggestion: Serve alongside a simple rice dish, roasted organic chicken or slow-cooked lamb. It is equally satisfying on its own as a light lunch with a drizzle of extra olive oil.

ingredients.name: organic tomato, seeds removed and finely diced
organic kale, stems removed, finely chopped
organic green cabbage, finely shredded and chopped small
organic cucumbers, seeds removed and finely diced
raw fermented apple cider vinegar, or to taste
Celtic sea salt, or to taste

steps: Fill a large bowl or clean sink with MEA structured water. Place all your whole vegetables including the carrots, tomato, parsley, kale, cabbage and cucumbers into the water and allow them to soak for 15 to 20 minutes. This step re-energises the produce, helps remove surface residues and wakes up the natural vitality of each ingredient. We never skip this step.

Lift the vegetables out of the water and lay them on a clean tea towel or paper towels. Pat everything dry gently. Damp vegetables will dilute your dressing and make the salad soggy, so take a moment to dry them well.

Prepare your cucumbers first. Slice them in half lengthways and use a small spoon to scoop out the seeds and watery centre. Discard the seeds. This keeps the salad crisp and stops it going watery in the bowl. Finely dice the cucumber flesh into small, even pieces.

Using a sharp knife, finely dice the carrots into very small pieces roughly the size of a grain of rice or a little larger. A sharp knife is important here. It gives you control, keeps the cuts clean and makes the whole process safer and faster.
Finely dice the tomato into small pieces, similar in size to the carrot and cucumber. Set aside.

Strip the kale leaves from their tough stems and discard the stems. Stack the leaves, roll them tightly and slice into thin ribbons, then turn and chop across to create small, fine pieces. Do the same with the cabbage, chopping until every piece is small and consistent.

Gather the parsley into a tight bunch and rock your sharp knife over it until it is very finely chopped. Do not rush this step. Finely chopped parsley distributes through the whole salad and delivers flavour in every single bite.
Add all the prepared vegetables and parsley into a large mixing bowl. Toss gently with clean hands or two large spoons to combine everything evenly.

Drizzle over the olive oil and the apple cider vinegar. Season with Celtic sea salt. Toss thoroughly to coat every piece. Taste and adjust the vinegar and salt to your liking. We tend to be generous with the apple cider vinegar because it lifts the whole salad beautifully.

Transfer to a serving bowl and bring it straight to the table. This salad is best served fresh. In our house it never lasts long and someone is always reaching for seconds before the main dish is finished.

images.caption: The fresh veggies take a bath in MEA water to energise them
Slice the veggies really small, its time consuming but very therapeutic
This salad is perfect for a Quinoa or rice dish as its micro sizes has a lovely mouth feel with similar sized foods

title: Slow-Cooked Beef Bone Broth Ramen
seoTitle: Slow-Cooked Beef Bone Broth Ramen Recipe
metaDesc: A deeply nourishing beef bone broth ramen made with pasture-raised bones, tallow-sautéed aromatics and real miso. Gluten free, dairy free and weeknight-friendly.
about: This bowl came together out of a desire to give our family something deeply nourishing on a school night without spending the whole weekend in the kitchen. We start with pasture-raised beef bones, let tallow carry the aromatics into something rich and golden, and finish with a spoonful of real miso that brings centuries of fermentation wisdom to a bowl that is ready when everyone sits down. It is the kind of ancient nourishment that happens to fit a modern Tuesday.
chefNote: The broth can be made two to three days ahead and stored in sealed glass jars in the refrigerator, where the fat will rise and set on top as a natural seal. Lift off the fat layer before reheating, or stir it back in for extra richness. The broth also freezes beautifully for up to three months, making it well worth doubling the batch while you have the bones and the time.
servingSuggestion: Serve immediately in deep, warmed bowls alongside extra tamari and a small dish of chilli oil or fermented chilli paste for those who like more heat. A simple side of kimchi or fermented vegetables adds another layer of gut-friendly nourishment to the meal.

ingredients.name: pasture-raised beef bones (knuckles, marrow or a mix)
spring onions, roughly chopped, plus extra to serve
white or brown rice miso paste (gluten free)
fine sea salt, plus more to taste
soft-boiled eggs, halved (optional, omit for dairy-free strict)

steps: Preheat your oven to 220°C fan-forced. Arrange the beef bones in a single layer on a large roasting tray and roast for 30 to 35 minutes, turning once halfway through, until they are deeply browned on the outside. This step builds the colour and depth that makes the broth genuinely satisfying rather than pale and thin.

Transfer the roasted bones to a large stockpot or slow cooker. Pour the apple cider vinegar over the bones and add the filtered cold water, making sure the bones are fully submerged. Let everything sit for 30 minutes without heat so the vinegar can begin drawing minerals from the bones before cooking starts.

While the bones are resting, melt two tablespoons of beef tallow in a heavy skillet over high heat. Place the halved onion and garlic cut-side down into the pan and leave them undisturbed for four to five minutes until the cut faces are well charred. This charring is not a mistake; it gives the broth its characteristic warmth and colour.

Add the charred onion and garlic to the pot along with the ginger rounds, chopped spring onions, celery and carrot. Bring everything to a gentle boil over medium-high heat, then reduce immediately to the lowest simmer your stove will allow. Skim off any foam or grey scum that rises to the surface during the first 20 minutes of simmering, as this gives you a cleaner, clearer broth.

Simmer the broth uncovered, or cover with the slow cooker lid on low, for a minimum of eight hours and up to twelve hours for maximum collagen extraction and flavour. If you are using a slow cooker, set it to low and let it work overnight. The broth is ready when it is deeply golden, aromatic and coats the back of a spoon lightly.

Strain the broth through a fine-mesh sieve or a colander lined with muslin cloth, discarding all solids. You should have approximately two litres of rich, concentrated broth. If you have more than that, return it to a clean pot and simmer uncovered for an additional 20 to 30 minutes to concentrate the flavour further.

Stir the tamari and coconut aminos into the hot strained broth and taste for seasoning, adding sea salt as needed. Keep the broth at a gentle simmer over low heat while you prepare the remaining components.

Place the miso paste into a small bowl and ladle about half a cup of hot broth over it. Whisk the mixture until the miso is fully dissolved, then pour it back into the main pot of broth and stir to combine. Do not allow the broth to boil vigorously after adding the miso, as high heat diminishes the beneficial enzymes and mellows the flavour too much.
Cook the rice ramen noodles according to the packet directions in a separate pot of salted boiling water, then drain and rinse briefly under warm water to stop them clumping. Set aside.

In the same skillet you used for the onion, melt the remaining tablespoon of tallow over medium-high heat. Add the sliced shiitake mushrooms in a single layer and cook without stirring for three minutes until golden on the underside, then toss and cook for another two minutes. Season lightly with sea salt and remove from the heat.
Blanch the bok choy halves by dropping them into the simmering broth for one to two minutes until just tender and bright green, then lift them out with a slotted spoon and set aside on a plate.

To serve, divide the noodles evenly among six deep bowls. Ladle the hot miso-seasoned broth generously over the noodles, then arrange the sautéed shiitake mushrooms, blanched bok choy, halved soft-boiled eggs and nori strips over the top. Finish each bowl with a small drizzle of toasted sesame oil, a scattering of toasted sesame seeds and chilli flakes if your family welcomes a little heat.
author: Mr Wellness

title: Soaked & Slow-Cooked Lentil Dal with Ghee Tarka
seoTitle: Soaked Lentil Dal with Ghee Tarka Recipe
metaDesc: A properly prepared red lentil dal with overnight soaking and a fragrant ghee tarka. An ancestral approach to a nourishing, family-friendly weeknight dinner.
about: Dal has been feeding families across generations not because it is simple, but because it is wise: soaking the lentils overnight breaks down the anti-nutrients that make legumes hard on digestion, and finishing the pot with a ghee tarka carries the fat-soluble compounds in those spices straight into the dish where the body can actually use them. We make this most weeks when the evening calls for something deeply nourishing without a great deal of fuss, and it is one of those meals the children ask for by name. Ancestral kitchens around the world understood that preparation time is part of the recipe, and this dal is a quiet reminder of that.
chefNote: Leftovers store very well in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days, and the dal actually deepens in flavour overnight. When reheating, add a small splash of water to loosen it and warm gently over a low heat, stirring often. You can also prepare a fresh small tarka to pour over reheated dal if you want to revive that fragrant top note.
servingSuggestion: Serve over warm basmati rice that has been cooked with a knob of ghee and a pinch of turmeric, or alongside sourdough flatbreads for scooping. A simple side of plain full-fat yoghurt and a cucumber and tomato salad rounds the meal out beautifully for a complete family dinner.

ingredients.name: red lentils, soaked overnight in cold filtered water
fine sea salt, plus more to taste
filtered water or homemade vegetable stock
whole cumin seeds, for the tarka
brown mustard seeds, for the tarka
fresh coriander leaves, roughly chopped, to serve
lemon, cut into wedges, to serve

steps: The evening before you plan to cook, place the red lentils in a large bowl and cover generously with cold filtered water. Allow them to soak for a minimum of eight hours and up to twelve. This soaking step is not optional in our kitchen: it neutralises phytic acid, reduces cooking time considerably, and makes the finished dal far gentler on the digestive system, particularly for children.

When you are ready to cook, drain the soaked lentils through a fine mesh sieve and rinse them thoroughly under cold running water until the water runs clear. Set them aside to drain while you prepare everything else.

Place a large, heavy-based pot or Dutch oven over a medium heat. Add the first measure of ghee and allow it to melt and shimmer without smoking. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring regularly, for eight to ten minutes until it is soft, translucent, and beginning to turn a light golden colour at the edges. Take your time here as a properly softened onion forms the flavour foundation for the entire dish.

Add the minced garlic and grated ginger to the pot and stir them through the onion. Cook for a further two minutes, stirring constantly, until the raw edge has disappeared and the mixture is fragrant.

Add the chopped tomatoes and stir everything together. Cook for five to six minutes, pressing the tomatoes gently with the back of your spoon as they soften, until they have broken down and formed a rough paste with the onion, garlic and ginger.

Add the ground turmeric, ground cumin, ground coriander, ground fenugreek and cayenne pepper directly to the tomato mixture. Stir continuously for sixty to ninety seconds, cooking the spices in the ghee and tomato base. This brief step, called bhunao in traditional cooking, is what lifts the dal from pleasant to deeply flavoured.

Add the drained and rinsed lentils to the pot and stir to coat them in the spiced tomato base. Pour in the filtered water or vegetable stock and add the sea salt. Stir well to combine, then bring the pot to a gentle boil over a medium-high heat.

Once boiling, reduce the heat to low, place a lid slightly ajar on the pot, and allow the dal to simmer gently for thirty-five to forty-five minutes, stirring every ten minutes or so. The lentils should gradually become very soft and begin to dissolve into the liquid, creating a thick, porridge-like consistency. If the dal thickens faster than you would like, add an extra splash of warm water and stir it through. Taste and adjust the salt at this point.

When the dal is fully cooked and sitting at your preferred consistency, prepare the tarka. Place a small heavy-based frying pan over a medium-high heat and add the second measure of ghee. Allow it to heat until it is clearly shimmering and hot. Add the whole cumin seeds and brown mustard seeds and let them sizzle in the ghee for about thirty seconds until the mustard seeds begin to pop.

Immediately add the curry leaves and dried red chillies to the pan. They will spit briefly so stand back and be ready. Swirl the pan once or twice and allow the spices to bloom in the ghee for a further twenty to thirty seconds. The kitchen should smell extraordinary at this point.

Pour the entire contents of the tarka pan directly over the cooked dal in one confident movement. You will hear a satisfying sizzle as it hits the surface. Stir the tarka through the dal gently to distribute it, then place the lid back on the pot for two minutes to allow the flavours to meld together.

Serve the dal in deep bowls, scattered generously with fresh coriander leaves and with lemon wedges alongside for squeezing over at the table. A good squeeze of lemon just before eating lifts all the earthy, spiced flavours beautifully.

title: Spelt Banana Choc Chip Muffins
seoTitle: Spelt Banana Choc Chip Muffins (Dairy Free)
metaDesc: These easy spelt banana choc chip muffins are dairy free, nut free, and naturally sweetened. Ready in 37 minutes and perfect for lunchboxes all week long.
about:
These nourishing banana muffins are a staple in our kitchen. Made with organic spelt flour, naturally sweetened with ripe bananas and a touch of maple syrup, and loaded with dairy free choc chips, they are completely dairy free and nut free. We make a batch on Sunday and they are gone by Tuesday.

Dairy free
Nut free
Chef's note
Store cooled muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days, or freeze them individually for up to 2 months. Pop one in a lunchbox frozen in the morning and it will be perfectly thawed by recess. These spelt banana choc chip muffins are a Sunday staple in our house. We make a big batch, pop them in an airtight container, and watch them disappear by Tuesday. Made with organic spelt flour, naturally sweetened with ripe bananas and a touch of maple syrup, and completely dairy free and nut free, they are the kind of wholesome snack we feel good about tucking into lunchboxes all week long.
chefNote: Store cooled muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days, or freeze them individually for up to 2 months. Pop one in a lunchbox frozen in the morning and it will be perfectly thawed by recess.
servingSuggestion: Enjoy warm from the oven with a drizzle of coconut butter, or pack them straight into lunchboxes as a wholesome school or work snack alongside a piece of fruit.

ingredients.name: dairy free organic choc chips, plus extra for topping

steps: Preheat your oven to 180 degrees Celsius fan forced. Line a 12 hole muffin tin with paper cases or grease each hole well with a little olive oil.
In a large mixing bowl, whisk together the spelt flour, baking soda, ground cinnamon, and sea salt until well combined. Set aside.
In a separate bowl, mash the ripe bananas thoroughly with a fork until smooth. The riper the bananas the better, lots of brown spots means more natural sweetness.
Add the olive oil, eggs, and maple syrup to the mashed bananas. Whisk everything together until the wet mixture is well combined.

Pour the wet ingredients into the bowl of dry ingredients. Using a spatula or wooden spoon, fold gently until just combined. Do not overmix. A few small lumps are perfectly fine and will give you a lighter muffin.
Fold through the dairy free choc chips, reserving a small handful for topping.
Divide the batter evenly between the 12 prepared muffin holes, filling each one about three quarters full. Scatter the reserved choc chips over the top of each muffin.
Bake for 20 to 22 minutes, or until the muffins are golden on top and a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean.
Remove from the oven and allow the muffins to cool in the tin for 5 minutes before transferring to a wire rack to cool completely.

title: Wheat-Free Chocolate Mud Cake
seoTitle: Wheat-Free Chocolate Mud Cake with Almond Flour
metaDesc: A rich, fudgy wheat-free chocolate mud cake made with almond flour and monk fruit sweetener. Gluten-free, lower-carb, and genuinely delicious for the whole family.
about: This is the cake we make when we want something genuinely indulgent that still fits with how we feed our family. Built on almond flour and sweetened with monk fruit, it delivers that dense, fudgy mud cake character without a grain of wheat in sight. Almond flour brings natural fat and protein to the crumb, which means every slice stays moist and satisfying in a way that processed gluten-free flour blends rarely manage.
chefNote: Store any leftover cake in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days. The texture actually improves on day two as the crumb settles and the flavours deepen. Bring individual slices to room temperature for 15 minutes before serving so the ganache softens and the cake loses its fridge chill.
servingSuggestion: Serve in generous slices with a dollop of lightly whipped cream or a spoonful of full-fat coconut yoghurt on the side. A small scattering of fresh raspberries cuts through the richness beautifully and makes the plate look genuinely lovely without any extra effort.

ingredients.name: monk fruit sweetener or erythritol blend, adjusted to taste
melted grass-fed butter, coconut oil, or light olive oil
milk of choice: full-fat dairy, coconut milk, or almond milk
good-quality dark chocolate (70% or higher), for the ganache
pouring cream or full-fat coconut cream, for the ganache

steps: Preheat your oven to 175°C (350°F) and position the rack in the centre. Grease a 20cm (8-inch) or 23cm (9-inch) round cake tin lightly with butter or coconut oil, then line the base and sides with baking paper so the cake releases cleanly once cooled.

In a large mixing bowl, whisk together the almond flour, cocoa powder, monk fruit sweetener, baking soda, salt, and espresso powder if you are using it. Almond flour tends to clump, so take a moment to work through any lumps with the whisk before moving on.

In a separate bowl, whisk the eggs, melted butter or oil, milk, and vanilla extract together until the mixture is smooth. Make sure your melted butter has cooled slightly before adding the eggs so you do not accidentally scramble them.

Pour the wet ingredients into the dry ingredients and stir with a spatula until just combined and no dry patches remain. The batter will be noticeably thicker than a conventional cake batter, which is entirely normal for almond flour. If you would like a little extra moisture, stir in one or two tablespoons of additional milk at this point.
If you are folding in optional sugar-free chocolate chips or roughly chopped nuts, do so now with a few gentle strokes so they are evenly distributed without overworking the batter.

Scrape the batter into the prepared tin and use the back of your spatula to smooth the top into an even layer. Almond flour batter is thick and will not spread itself during baking the way a thinner batter would.

Bake for 28 to 35 minutes. A 20cm tin will generally need the longer end of that range, while a 23cm tin tends to be done closer to 28 minutes. Start checking at the 27-minute mark by inserting a toothpick into the centre of the cake. It is ready when the toothpick comes out with just a few moist crumbs clinging to it. A completely clean toothpick usually means the cake has gone a little too long, as almond flour cakes can dry out quickly if overbaked.

Remove the cake from the oven and allow it to cool in the tin on a wire rack for 10 to 15 minutes before attempting to turn it out. Almond flour cakes are more fragile when warm than wheat-based cakes, so this resting time matters. Once the tin is cool enough to handle, carefully invert the cake onto the wire rack, peel away the baking paper, and leave it to cool completely before adding the ganache.

While the cake cools, make the ganache. Break the dark chocolate into a small heatproof bowl. Heat the cream or coconut cream in a small saucepan over low heat until it just begins to steam and tiny bubbles appear around the edges, then pour it over the chocolate. Leave it to sit undisturbed for two minutes, then stir gently from the centre outward until the ganache is glossy and completely smooth. Allow it to cool at room temperature for 15 to 20 minutes until it thickens to a pourable but not runny consistency.

Once the cake is fully cooled, pour the ganache over the top and use a spatula or the back of a spoon to ease it gently toward the edges, allowing it to drip down the sides naturally. Leave the ganache to set for at least 20 minutes before slicing and serving.

title: Wild Fermented Beetroot and Goat's Cheese Salad
seoTitle: Wild Fermented Beetroot & Goat's Cheese Salad
metaDesc: A gut-loving wild fermented beetroot and goat's cheese salad made from Australian produce. A probiotic-rich main that is as nourishing as it is beautiful.
about: This salad came about because we wanted something that could hold its own as a proper main, not just a side thought, and the lacto-fermented beetroot we had sitting quietly in the pantry turned out to be exactly the thing that made it sing. Wild fermentation is one of the oldest ways humans have preserved the harvest, and when you use Australian-grown beetroot, the good bacteria that develop are genuinely local to the soil and season. The result is a plate full of living cultures, earthy sweetness, creamy goat's cheese and enough substance to carry a weeknight dinner with ease.
chefNote: The fermented beetroot can be made up to three weeks in advance and kept sealed in the refrigerator, making this a genuinely practical main for busy weeks. If goat's cheese is not to everyone's taste at the table, a good quality Persian feta works beautifully in its place and carries a similar creamy, tangy quality that balances the beetroot.
servingSuggestion: Serve with thick slices of sourdough bread spread with good butter, or alongside a simple roasted chicken if you want to add more protein to the meal. A chilled glass of skin-contact wine or a sparkling water with a squeeze of orange is a lovely pairing alongside.

ingredients.name: Australian beetroot, scrubbed and trimmed (about 800g total)
fine sea salt (non-iodised), plus extra to taste
navel orange, segmented with pith removed

ingredients.amount: Sea salt and freshly cracked pepper
ingredients.name: to season the dressing

steps: Begin the wild fermentation at least five days before you plan to serve the salad, as the beetroot needs time to develop its full flavour and probiotic culture. Wash a large glass jar (approximately 1.5 litre capacity) thoroughly and rinse it well with very hot water to clean it without introducing any soap residue that might inhibit fermentation.

Dissolve the sea salt in the litre of filtered water, stirring well until the salt is completely incorporated. It is important to use non-chlorinated water here, as chlorine in tap water can prevent the beneficial bacteria from doing their work. If you only have tap water available, leave it uncovered on the bench overnight and the chlorine will dissipate.
Peel the beetroot and cut them into batons or wedges roughly one centimetre thick. You want them substantial enough to hold their texture through the fermentation process rather than turning soft.

Pack the beetroot pieces firmly into the clean jar, tucking the garlic cloves, peppercorns and thyme sprigs in among the layers as you go. The aromatics are not just for flavour; they help create a more complex ferment.

Pour the prepared salt brine over the beetroot until everything is completely submerged, leaving about two centimetres of space at the top of the jar. It is essential that the beetroot stays below the surface of the brine throughout fermentation, as any pieces exposed to air can develop surface mould. Use a small zip-lock bag filled with extra brine, or a clean stone, placed on top of the beetroot to keep everything weighted down.

Cover the jar loosely with a cloth secured with a rubber band, or use a lid placed loosely on top to allow gases to escape. Place the jar on a plate to catch any brine that bubbles over, and leave it at room temperature, out of direct sunlight, ideally somewhere between 18 and 22 degrees Celsius.

After two days you should notice small bubbles beginning to form, which is the sign that lacto-fermentation is underway. Taste the brine at day three and again at day five. The beetroot is ready when it tastes pleasantly tangy, still earthy and sweet but with a bright, lively acidity that makes your mouth water. In warmer weather fermentation can move faster, so start tasting from day three. Once it reaches a flavour you love, seal the jar with a lid and move it to the refrigerator, where it will keep for several weeks.

When you are ready to assemble the salad, remove the fermented beetroot from the jar with a clean fork or tongs and set it aside. Reserve two tablespoons of the brine for the dressing, as it carries all of that wonderful cultured flavour and acts as a natural acidulant.

Make the dressing by whisking together the olive oil, reserved beetroot brine, raw honey and Dijon mustard in a small bowl until the mixture is emulsified and cohesive. Taste it and adjust with a little sea salt and cracked pepper. The brine is already salty, so add any extra salt carefully.

Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry frying pan over medium heat for two to three minutes, shaking the pan regularly, until they are golden and beginning to pop. Remove them from the heat and allow them to cool on a plate.

Combine the rocket and baby spinach in a large wide serving bowl and toss them gently together so the greens are evenly distributed. Arrange the fermented beetroot pieces across the top, followed by the orange segments and the finely sliced red onion.

Scatter the crumbled goat's cheese across the salad, then add the toasted walnuts and the cooled pumpkin seeds. Drizzle the dressing over everything in a generous, even pour, and finish with a few extra cracks of black pepper. Bring the salad to the table and toss it lightly at the last moment, or serve it arranged as it is and let everyone help themselves.
